**(Surah At-Tahrim)**
Twelve verses, Madani

﷽ (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾

﷽ (In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful)

﴿O Prophet, why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you, seeking the pleasure of your wives? God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful.﴾

As for its connection with what precedes it: it lies in the sharing of rulings specific to women, and in the sharing of address concerning divorce (talaq) at the beginning of that surah with the address concerning prohibition at the beginning of this surah. Since divorce, in most of its forms, or in all of them as is the view of some scholars, includes the prohibition of what God has made lawful. As for the connection of the first with the latter: what is mentioned at the end of that surah points to the greatness of the majesty of God, the Exalted, just as it points to His perfect power and perfect knowledge, since the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the wonders and marvels within them, is dependent upon them. And the greatness of the Majesty is incompatible with the power to prohibit what God has made lawful. For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿Why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you﴾.

They differed concerning what the Prophet ﷺ had prohibited for himself. In al-Kashshaf it is said: it is related that he, upon him be blessings and peace, was alone with Mariyah on the day of Aisha, and Hafsa came to know of it. So he said to her: "Keep this secret for me, for I have prohibited Mariyah upon myself, and I give you good news that Abu Bakr and Umar will rule over my community after me." So she informed Aisha of it, and the two were close friends. It was also said that he was alone with her on the day of Hafsa, and he pleased her with this and asked her to keep it secret, but she did not keep it. So he divorced her and withdrew from his wives, and he remained twenty-nine nights in the house of Mariyah. It is also related that Umar said to her: "If there were any good in the family of al-Khattab, he would not have divorced you." Then Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and said: "Take her back, for she fasts often and prays much at night, and she is among your wives in Paradise." It is also related that he did not divorce her, but merely mentioned her divorce. It is also related that he, upon him be blessings and peace, drank honey in the house of Zaynab bint Jahsh, so Aisha and Hafsa conspired, and said to him: "We smell from you the odor of maghafir (a foul-smelling gum)." The Messenger of God ﷺ disliked the smell of the mouth, so he prohibited honey. Its meaning then is: "Why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you, of the slave women you own, or of the honey?" The first view is the statement of al-Hasan, Mujahid, Qatadah, al-Sha'bi and Masruq. It is also the narration of Thabit from Anas. Masruq said: The Prophet ﷺ prohibited his umm walad (a slave woman who bore him a child) and swore that he would not approach her, so God the Exalted revealed this verse. It was said to him: "As for the prohibition, it is permissible; and as for the oath you swore, God has prescribed for you the expiation of your oaths." Al-Sha'bi said: With the prohibition there was an oath, so he was rebuked for the prohibition, and only the oath is expiated. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿God has already prescribed﴾, to the end of the verse.

The author of al-Nazm said: His saying ﴿why do you prohibit﴾ is an interrogation in the sense of disapproval, and disapproval from God the Exalted is a prohibition. The prohibition of the lawful is disliked, and the lawful is not made unlawful except by the prohibition of God the Exalted. His saying the Exalted ﴿seeking the pleasure of your wives﴾, where "tabtaghi" (you seek) is a circumstantial clause (hal) that came in the form of the present tense. The meaning is: "Why do you prohibit, seeking the pleasure of your wives?" In al-Kashshaf it is said: "tabtaghi" is either an explanation of "tuharrimu" (you prohibit), or a circumstantial clause, or a new sentence. This is a slip from him, because no one has the right to prohibit what God has made lawful. ﴿God is Most Forgiving, Most Merciful﴾: He has forgiven you what preceded of the slip; "Merciful" means He has shown you mercy and did not hold you to account for it. Then in the verse there are several discussions.

**First discussion:** The statement ﴿why do you prohibit what God has made lawful for you﴾ seems to imply that this address is by way of rebuke, and addressing the one described, who is the Prophet, contradicts that because it contains honour and exaltation. How then is this? We say: the apparent meaning is that this address is not by way of rebuke, but by way of alerting that what proceeded from him was not as it should have been.

**Second discussion:** Prohibiting what God the Exalted has made lawful is impossible, because making lawful means giving preference to the side of permissibility, and prohibiting means giving preference to the side of prohibition, and there is no room for these two preferences to coexist. How then can it be said: ﴿why do you prohibit what God has made lawful﴾? We say: what is meant by this prohibition is abstaining from benefiting from the wives, not believing that it has become unlawful after God the Exalted made it lawful. So the Prophet ﷺ abstained from benefiting from them while believing that they were lawful. Whoever believes that this prohibition is the very prohibition of what God the Exalted has made lawful has disbelieved. So how can such a thing be attributed to the Messenger ﷺ?

**Third discussion:** If it is asked: what is the ruling on prohibiting what is lawful? We say: the imams have differed about it. Abu Hanifa holds it to be an oath in every case, and he considers the benefit intended in what one prohibits. So if one prohibits food, he has sworn to not eat it; or a slave woman, then to not have intercourse with her; or a wife, then it is ila' (a vow of abstention from intercourse) concerning her, if he has no intention. If he intended zihar (a pre-Islamic form of divorce by comparing the wife to a forbidden relative), then it is zihar; if he intended divorce, then it is an irrevocable divorce (talaq ba'in). Likewise if he intended two, and if he intended three, then it is as he intended. If he says: "I intended a lie," he is believed between himself and his Lord, but in judgment he is not believed in annulling the ila'. If he says: "Everything lawful for me is unlawful for me," then it applies to food and drink if he has no intention; otherwise it applies to what he intended. Al-Shafi'i does not regard it as an oath, but as a cause (sabab) for expiation (kaffarah) only with regard to women. If he intended divorce, it is revocable (raj'i) according to him. As for the disagreement of the Companions concerning it, it is as stated in al-Kashshaf, so there is no need for us to mention it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 66, verses 2–3:

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths. God is your Protector, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.﴾ ﴿And when the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives, and she spread it, and God revealed it to him, he made known part of it and ignored part of it. Then, when he informed her of it, she said, "Who told you this?" He said, "The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me."﴾

﴿God has already ordained for you.﴾ Muqatil said: "God has already made clear," as in His saying: ﴿A surah which We sent down and ordained﴾ (al-Nur: 1). The rest said: "He has made it obligatory." The author of al-Nazm (a work on the composition and coherence of the Qur'an) said: "When it is connected with ʿala (upon), it admits only the meaning of obligation, as in His saying: ﴿We already know what We have ordained for them﴾ (al-Ahzab: 50). When it is connected with al-lam (for), it admits both meanings."

His saying: ﴿the dissolution of your oaths﴾ means their dissolution through expiation (kaffarah). Tahillah is on the pattern tafilah, and its root is tahlilah. The dissolution of an oath has two senses:

First: its dissolution through expiation, as in this verse.

Second: that it is used in the sense of a small amount. This is the more common usage, as it is related in the hadith: "Not one of them will enter the Fire except for the dissolution of an oath" (la yalija al-nar illa tahillata al-qasam), meaning a brief period of time.

It is also read as "the expiation of your oaths" (kaffarata aymanikum). A group of the exegetes reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) swore not to approach his slave-girl, so God made known to him what He had prescribed as the expiation of an oath. Saʿid ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbas that "the forbidden (al-haram) is an oath," meaning that if a man says, "You are forbidden to me" and does not intend divorce or zihar, this phrase necessitates the expiation of an oath.

﴿God is your Protector﴾, that is, your Guardian and Helper. ﴿He is the All-Knowing﴾ of His creation, ﴿the All-Wise﴾ in what He has ordained of His rulings.

His saying: ﴿And when the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives﴾ refers to what he confided to Hafsah concerning forbidding the slave-girl upon himself, and he asked her to keep it secret. It is also said: when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw jealousy in Hafsah's face, he wished to appease her, so he confided two things to her: the forbidding of the slave-girl upon himself, and the good news that the caliphate after him would belong to Abu Bakr and her father ʿUmar. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

His saying: ﴿and she spread it﴾ means she informed ʿAʾishah of it. ﴿And God revealed it to him﴾ means He informed His Prophet of Hafsah's words to ʿAʾishah. The Prophet (ﷺ) then informed Hafsah of some of what she had said, which is His saying: ﴿he made known part of it﴾ to Hafsah, ﴿and ignored part of it﴾, not informing her that she had told ʿAʾishah, out of generosity and forbearance. What he ignored was the mention of the caliphate of Abu Bakr and ʿUmar.

It is also read as ʿarafa (without the doubling), meaning "requited for it," from your saying to the wrongdoer: "I will surely repay you for that, and I have known what you did." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God knows what is in them﴾ (al-Nisa': 63), meaning He will requite them, and He knows what is in the hearts of all creation.

His saying: ﴿So when he informed her of it, she said﴾ — Hafsah — ﴿"Who told you this?" He said, "The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me."﴾ He described Him as "All-Aware" after describing Him as "All-Knowing," because in khabir there is an intensity that is not in ʿalim.

There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: How does His saying ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ relate to His saying ﴿Why do you forbid what God has made lawful for you?﴾ (al-Tahrim: 1)? We say: it relates to it because the forbidding of a woman was regarded as an oath. So if a man says to his wife, "You are forbidden to me," it is an oath, and by mentioning it he becomes one who has sworn to abstain (mu'li), and he must make expiation.

The second issue: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿God has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths﴾ is that the Prophet had made an oath. Did the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, make expiation for it? We say: according to al-Hasan, he did not make expiation, because God had forgiven him what he had done before and after; rather, it was instruction for the believers. According to Muqatil, he freed a slave as expiation for forbidding Mariyah.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If you two turn in repentance to God, your hearts have indeed inclined, and if you back each other against him, then indeed God is his protector, and Gabriel, and the righteous among the believers, and the angels after that are his supporters.﴾ ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you: submissive, believing, devout, repentant, worshipful, who fast, previously married and virgins.﴾

His saying: ﴿If you two turn in repentance to God﴾ is an address to 'A'isha and Hafsa in the manner of iltifat (a shift in grammatical person), so that it is more forceful in rebuking them both and in calling them to repent of cooperating against the Messenger of God (ﷺ) by causing him harm. ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾ means they deviated and turned away from the truth, which is the right of the Messenger, peace be upon him. That is a great right, in which one who falls short even slightly deserves reproach. The answer to the conditional clause is omitted, being understood, and the sense is: "It would have been better for you both." By the plural in His saying ﴿your hearts﴾ is meant the dual. Al-Farra' said: The plural was chosen over the dual because most of the limbs in a human being come in pairs, such as the two hands, the two feet and the two eyes. Since most of them follow this pattern, the singular of such a pair, when it is added to a dual, is treated as a dual, and this has already been mentioned.

His saying: ﴿And if you back each other against him﴾ means if you cooperate against the Prophet (ﷺ) by causing him harm. ﴿Then indeed God is his protector﴾ means that this backing up by you two does not harm him. ﴿Mawlah﴾ means his guardian and helper. ﴿Gabriel﴾ is the chief of the karubiyyun (the angels closest to God). He is mentioned alongside the angels after the general mention, singling him out among the angels to honour him and to show his high rank. ﴿And the righteous among the believers.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: He means Abu Bakr and 'Umar, who support the Prophet (ﷺ) against whoever opposes him, and who are his helpers. This is also the view of Muqatil. Al-Dahhak said: the best of the believers. It was also said: whoever among the believers is righteous, that is, every believer who has faith and does righteous deeds. It was also said: whoever among them is free of hypocrisy. It was also said: all the prophets. It was also said: the caliphs. It was also said: the Companions. The word ṣāliḥ here stands in for the plural, and it is permissible to mean by it both the singular and the plural.

His saying: ﴿And the angels after that﴾ means after the presence of God, Gabriel and the righteous believers. ﴿Ẓahīr﴾ means a group that backs the Prophet (ﷺ) and assists him. Ẓahīr here has the sense of ẓuhara (plural of supporters), as in His saying: ﴿And how excellent those are as companions﴾ (al-Nisa’: 69). Al-Farra' said: "And the angels, after the support of these, are a ẓahīr." Abu 'Ali said: The form fa'īl has come in the singular while meaning plurality, as in His saying: ﴿A close friend will not ask a close friend﴾ and ﴿They will be made to see them﴾ (al-Ma'arij: 10–11).

Then He warned his wives with His saying: ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you.﴾ The exegetes said: "It may be" (‘asā) from God is binding. The people of Kufa read ﴿yubdilahu﴾ with the lighter form. Yet God knew that He would not divorce them, but He informed of His power, that if he divorced them He would replace them with better ones, as a warning to them. The more common form for ﴿ṭallaqakunna﴾ is with the clear pronunciation of the consonants, but Abu 'Amr assimilated the qāf into the kāf, because both are letters of the mouth.

Then He described the wives He would give in exchange, saying: ﴿Submissive﴾ means humbly obedient to God in worship. ﴿Believing﴾ means affirming the oneness of God, sincerely. ﴿Devout﴾ means obedient. It was also said: standing in prayer at night. This is closer to the meaning, because He mentions "those who fast" (al-sā'iḥāt) after this, and al-sā'iḥāt means those who fast by day. So it follows that night prayer should be combined with fasting by day. It has also been read as sayyiḥāt, which is more emphatic. It was said of the one who fasts that he is a sā'ih (traveller), because the traveller has no provisions with him, so he keeps abstaining until he finds someone to feed him, and so the faster is compared to one who abstains until the time of breaking his fast arrives. It was also said: sā'iḥāt means emigrants.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Previously married and virgins,﴾ because the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), in this world and the next, are partly previously married and partly virgins, so the mention follows what actually happened. In this there is an indication that the Prophet's (ﷺ) marriages were not according to desire and inclination, but according to the seeking of God's good pleasure, exalted is He.

There are several discussions concerning the verse:

The first discussion: His saying ﴿after that﴾ is a glorification of the angels and of their supporting role. It has been read as tazāhara, tatazāhara and taẓharā.

The second discussion: How can those who replace them be better than them, when there were no women on the face of the earth better than the Mothers of the Believers? We say: If the Messenger divorces them for their disobedience to him and their harming him, they will no longer possess that quality, and others who possess these attributes together with obedience to the Messenger of God will be better than them.

[p. 41]

The third discussion: His saying ﴿submissive, believing﴾ seems to imply repetition, since "Muslim" and "believer" are the same. We say: Islam is affirmation by the tongue, and faith is affirmation by the heart, and the two may not coincide. So His saying ﴿submissive, believing﴾ confirms affirmation by both heart and tongue.

The fourth discussion: God said ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ with the conjunctive waw, but He did not say it with the conjunctive waw for the other attributes. We say: In al-Kashshaf it is said that these are two contrary attributes, which do not come together in the same person as the other attributes do.

The fifth discussion: He mentioned the previously married in a context of praise, though being previously married is among the things that reduce men's desire for them. We say: It is possible that some previously married women are better, in the Messenger's estimation, than some virgins, because of their distinction in wealth, beauty, lineage, or all of these, for example. If that is so, then the mention of the previously married does not detract from the praise, since it may refer to the kind of previously married women we have described.

The first discussion: His saying ﴿after that﴾ is a glorification of the angels and of their supporting role. It has been read as tazāhara, tatazāhara and taẓharā.

The second discussion: How can those who replace them be better than them, when there were no women on the face of the earth better than the Mothers of the Believers? We say: If the Messenger divorces them for their disobedience to him and their harming him, they will no longer possess that quality, and others who possess these attributes together with obedience to the Messenger of God will be better than them.

[p. 41]

The third discussion: His saying ﴿submissive, believing﴾ seems to imply repetition, since "Muslim" and "believer" are the same. We say: Islam is affirmation by the tongue, and faith is affirmation by the heart, and the two may not coincide. So His saying ﴿submissive, believing﴾ confirms affirmation by both heart and tongue.

The fourth discussion: God said ﴿previously married and virgins﴾ with the conjunctive waw, but He did not say it with the conjunctive waw for the other attributes. We say: In al-Kashshaf it is said that these are two contrary attributes, which do not come together in the same person as the other attributes do.

The fifth discussion: He mentioned the previously married in a context of praise, though being previously married is among the things that reduce men's desire for them. We say: It is possible that some previously married women are better, in the Messenger's estimation, than some virgins, because of their distinction in wealth, beauty, lineage, or all of these, for example. If that is so, then the mention of the previously married does not detract from the praise, since it may refer to the kind of previously married women we have described.

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is men and stones, over which are angels, harsh and severe, who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them and do what they are commanded.﴾ ﴿O you who have disbelieved, do not make excuses today. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾

﴿Protect yourselves﴾ means: by refraining from what Allah the Exalted has forbidden you. Muqatil said: that the Muslim should discipline himself and his family, commanding them to good and forbidding them from evil. In al-Kashshaf it is said: ﴿protect yourselves﴾ by abandoning sins and performing acts of obedience; ﴿and your families﴾ by holding them accountable to what you hold yourselves accountable for. It was also said: ﴿protect yourselves﴾ from what your souls call you to, since the souls command evil. It was recited as (wa-ahlūkum) [and your families], in coordination with the waw of (quū) [protect], and the coordination is good because of the intervening element. As for ﴿fire﴾, it is a type of fire that is kindled only with men and stones. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that it is the stones of sulphur, because it is the most intensely hot of things when it is set alight. It was recited as (wuqūduhā) with a ḍammah. His saying ﴿over it are angels﴾ refers to the nineteen guardians (al-Zabaniyah) and their helpers. ﴿Harsh and severe﴾: in their bodies there is harshness and severity, meaning roughness and strength; or in their actions there is roughness and coarseness. It is not far-fetched that they have these attributes in their creation, or in their actions, by being severe against the enemies of Allah and merciful toward the friends of Allah, as He the Exalted said: ﴿Severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ (al-Fath: 29). His saying the Exalted: ﴿and do what they are commanded﴾ indicates their severity because of the command's standing, such that no compassion takes them in executing the commands of Allah the Exalted and in exacting retribution upon His enemies. In this is an indication that the angels are charged in the Hereafter with what Allah the Exalted has commanded them and with what He forbids them, and disobedience from them is opposition to the command and the prohibition.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿O you who have disbelieved, do not make excuses today﴾: when He mentioned the severity of the punishment by the Fire, and the severity of the angels in exacting retribution upon the enemies, He said: ﴿do not make excuses today﴾, meaning it is said to them: do not make excuses today; for excuse is repentance, and repentance is not accepted after entering the Fire, so excuse will not benefit you. His saying the Exalted: ﴿You are only being recompensed for what you used to do﴾ means: your evil deeds alone have necessitated for you the punishment, by way of wisdom. In the verse there are several discussions:

The first discussion: He, the Exalted, addressed the polytheists in His saying: ﴿But if you do not, and you will never do, then fear the Fire whose fuel is men and stones﴾, and said: ﴿it is prepared for the disbelievers﴾ (al-Baqarah: 24), making it prepared for the disbelievers. So what is the meaning of addressing the believers with it? We say: the sinners, although their levels are above the levels of the disbelievers, are with the disbelievers in one abode. So it was said to those who believed: ﴿protect yourselves﴾ by avoiding sinfulness and by being neighbors to those for whom this Fire is prepared. And it is not far-fetched that He commands them to guard against apostasy.

The second discussion: how can the angels be harsh and severe when they are of the spirits? We say: harshness and severity are according to attributes, since they are of the spirits, not according to essence; and this is the closest of the sayings concerning the matter.

The third discussion: His saying the Exalted: ﴿who do not disobey Allah in what He commands them﴾ has the meaning of His saying: ﴿and do what they are commanded﴾. So what is the benefit of the mention? We say: this is not the same meaning as that; for the meaning of the first is that they accept His commands, bind themselves to them, and do not deny them, and the meaning of the second is that they (carry out) what they are commanded. Thus al-Zamakhshari mentioned it in al-Kashshaf.

[Page 43 begins at "the Mu'tazila"]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who have believed, repent to God with sincere repentance. Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow, on the Day when God will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him. Their light will run before them and on their right. They will say, "Our Lord, perfect our light for us and forgive us. Indeed, You are over all things competent."﴾ ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾

His saying, ﴿nasuhan﴾ (sincere), means: a repentance that reaches the utmost in sincerity (nush). Al-Farra' said: "Nasuhan is an attribute of repentance, and the meaning is a repentance that advises its performer to abandon returning to what he has repented of. It is the truthful, sincere repentance, by which they advise their own souls." It is also reported from 'Asim that it is read as nusuhan with a ḍammah on the nūn, which is a verbal noun (maṣdar) of the pattern of ʿuqūd (contracts). One says: nasaḥtu lahu nuṣḥan wa-naṣāḥatan wa-nuṣūḥan (I advised him sincerely). In al-Kashshaf (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari), it is said: "Repentance is described as sincere by way of metaphorical attribution (al-isnad al-majazi), namely that they repent of the vices, regretting them with the utmost regret, and do not return to them." It was also said: it is from naṣāḥat al-thawb, meaning its stitching (mending a garment). And ﴿ʿasā rabbukum﴾ (perhaps your Lord) is God, exalted is He, giving His servants hope.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The Day when God will not disgrace the Prophet﴾: the phrase is governed by ﴿yudkhilakum﴾ (He will admit you). And ﴿lā yukhzī﴾ (will not disgrace) is an indirect reproach to those whom God has disgraced among the people of disbelief and wickedness, and a call for the believers to praise God because He protected them from the like of their condition. Then the Mu'tazila (rationalist school) took hold of His saying, ﴿The Day when God will not disgrace the Prophet﴾, and said: "Disgrace (ikhzā') occurs through punishment. He has promised that He will not punish those who believed. If the people of grave sins were among the believers, we would not fear punishment for them." The People of the Sunna (Ahl al-Sunna) answered this by saying: God promised the people of faith that He would not disgrace them. [The phrase] ﴿wa-alladhina amanu﴾ (and those who believed) is the beginning of a new clause, and its predicate is ﴿yasʿā﴾ (runs), or ﴿lā yukhzī﴾. Then some of the People of the Sunna stop at His saying, ﴿The Day when God will not disgrace the Prophet﴾, meaning: He will not disgrace him by rejecting his intercession. Ikhzā' is exposure (fadīḥa), meaning He will not expose them before the disbelievers. It is permissible that He punishes them in a way that the disbelievers do not witness. His saying, ﴿bayna aydihim﴾ (before them), means during walking, and ﴿wa-bi-aymanihim﴾ (and on their right), means during the reckoning, because they are given their book in their right hands, and in it is light and good. The light runs before them at the place where their feet are set down, and on their right, because behind them and on their left is the path of the disbelievers.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, perfect our light for us"﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said: "They say this when the light of the hypocrites is extinguished, out of solicitude." It is reported from al-Hasan that He, exalted is He, completes their light for them, but they supplicate in order to draw near to the presence of God, exalted is He, like His saying: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin﴾ (Muhammad: 19), while he is already forgiven. It was also said: the lowest of them in rank is the one whose light is only sufficient to see the place where his foot treads, because light is in proportion to deeds, so they ask for its completion. It was also said: the foremost to Paradise pass over the Sirat like lightning, some like the wind, and some crawling and dragging themselves. These are the ones who say, ﴿Our Lord, perfect our light for us﴾. This is what al-Kashshaf says.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾: He mentioned the hypocrites separately, although the word disbelievers includes the hypocrites. ﴿And be harsh with them﴾ means: be severe with them. Struggle (mujahada) may be by fighting, and it may be by argument, sometimes by the tongue and sometimes by the spear. It was also said: strive against them by enforcing the prescribed punishments (hudud) upon them, because they are the ones who commit the grave sins, since the Companions of the Messenger were protected from them. ﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾, whose explanation has already passed. There are issues in this verse:

The first issue: How is ﴿O you who have believed﴾ connected to what came before, which is His saying: ﴿O you who have disbelieved﴾ (al-Tahrim: 7)? We say: He alerted them to averting the punishment on that Day by repentance in this world, since on that Day repentance will not benefit. In this there is a subtle point: alerting them to averting [punishment] after the warning (tarhib) of what preceded yields encouragement (targhib) by mentioning their states and the blessings and honour bestowed upon them.

The second issue: He will not disgrace the Prophet on that Day, nor those who believed, so what is the need for His saying ﴿maʿahu﴾ (with him)? We say: it serves to convey togetherness, meaning: God will not disgrace the whole group whose light runs [before them]. This is a great benefit, for togetherness between those who believed and their Prophet is an honour and exaltation for them.

The third issue: His saying, ﴿and forgive us﴾, seems to imply that sin is necessary for each of the believers, and sin cannot be necessary. We say: it is possible that the request for forgiveness is for what is necessarily part of every sin, namely shortcoming in service, and shortcoming is necessary for every one of the believers.

The fourth issue: God said at the beginning of the surah: ﴿O Prophet, why do you forbid﴾ (al-Tahrim: 1), and after it: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers﴾. He addressed him by his attribute, which is "the Prophet," not by his name, like His saying to Adam: "O Adam," to Moses: "O Moses," and to Jesus: "O Jesus." We say: He addressed him with this attribute to indicate his superiority over them, and this is evident.

The fifth issue: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And their refuge is Hell﴾, indicates that their destination is absolutely "wretched is the destination," because the absolute indicates permanence, whereas the non-absolute does not indicate it, since [the non-absolute] purifies them from their sins.

Then Allah the Exalted said: "Allah presents an example for those who disbelieve: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, so the two men could not avail them at all against Allah. And it was said, 'Enter the Fire along with those who enter.'" "And Allah presents an example for those who believe: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, 'My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds, and save me from the wrongdoing people.'"

His saying, "Allah presents an example" (ḍaraba Allāhu mathalan), meaning: He clarified their condition by way of parable, that they will be punished for their disbelief and their enmity toward the believers with the punishment of their like, without any shielding or favoritism. Their kinship with their prophet does not benefit them, nor does what they had of ties of blood between them and their Prophet, nor their denial of the Messenger ﷺ regarding what he brought from Allah, nor their persistence in it, nor their severing of relations, and their making of kinsmen among the strangers, indeed even further removed than them. Even if the believer to whom the disbeliever is connected is a prophet, as in the case of the wives of Noah and Lot, when they betrayed the two of them, these two Messengers did not avail them, and it was said to them on the Last Day: "Enter the Fire." Then He clarified the condition of the Muslims: that the connection of the disbelievers does not harm them, as in the case of the wife of Pharaoh and her station with Allah the Exalted, despite her being the wife of a wrongdoer, one of the enemies of Allah the Exalted, and Mary, daughter of ʿImrān, and what she was given of honor in this world and the Hereafter, and her being chosen above the women of the worlds, even though her people were disbelievers. Within these two parables there is an allusion to the two mothers of the believers, Ḥafṣa and ʿĀʾisha, regarding what had transpired from them, and a warning to them in the strongest and most severe manner, because the parable includes mention of disbelief. And He presented another example in the wife of Pharaoh, Āsiya daughter of Muzāḥim. It is said she was the paternal aunt of Moses, peace be upon him. She believed when she heard the story of Moses casting his staff and its swallowing [the magicians' ropes]; so Pharaoh tortured her severely because of her faith. It is related from Abū Hurayra that he pegged her down with four stakes, faced her toward the sun, and placed upon her a great rock. She said, "My Lord, save me from Pharaoh," and her soul was raised to Paradise, and the rock fell upon a body with no soul in it. Al-Ḥasan said: He raised her to Paradise where she eats and drinks. It is also said: when she said, "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise," she saw her house in Paradise being built for her, and it is of a single pearl. Allah knows best how it is and what it is.

There are discussions regarding the verse:

The first discussion: What is the benefit of His saying, "from Our servants" (min ʿibādinā)? We say it has two aspects:

The first: to honor them, as has passed.

The second: to show that the servant is not preferred over the other in His sight except by righteousness.

The second discussion: What was their betrayal? We say: it was their hypocrisy, their concealment of disbelief, and their backing of the two Messengers' opponents. The wife of Noah said to her people, "He is a madman," and the wife of Lot used to inform on the arrival of Abraham's guest. It is not permissible that their betrayal was in fornication. From Ibn ʿAbbās: "The wife of a prophet never committed adultery at all." It is also said their betrayal was in religion.

The third discussion: What is the meaning of combining "ʿindaka" (with You) and "fī al-Janna" (in Paradise)? We say: she sought nearness to Allah's mercy, then specified the place of nearness by her saying "in Paradise"; or she intended the elevation of her rank in the Paradise of the Abode, which is closest to the Throne.

They were under two of Our righteous servants, but they betrayed them, so the two men could not avail them at all against Allah. And it was said, 'Enter the Fire along with those who enter.'" Even if the believer to whom the disbeliever is connected is a prophet, as in the case of the wives of Noah and Lot, when they betrayed the two of them, these two Messengers did not avail them, and it was said to them on the Last Day: "Enter the Fire." Then He clarified the condition of the Muslims: that the connection of the disbelievers does not harm them, as in the case of the wife of Pharaoh and her station with Allah the Exalted, despite her being the wife of a wrongdoer, one of the enemies of Allah the Exalted, and Mary, daughter of ʿImrān, and what she was given of honor in this world and the Hereafter, and her being chosen above the women of the worlds, even though her people were disbelievers. Within these two parables there is an allusion to the two mothers of the believers, Ḥafṣa and ʿĀʾisha, regarding what had transpired from them, and a warning to them in the strongest and most severe manner, because the parable includes mention of disbelief. And He presented another example in the wife of Pharaoh, Āsiya daughter of Muzāḥim. It is said she was the paternal aunt of Moses, peace be upon him. She believed when she heard the story of Moses casting his staff and its swallowing [the magicians' ropes]; so Pharaoh tortured her severely because of her faith. It is related from Abū Hurayra that he pegged her down with four stakes, faced her toward the sun, and placed upon her a great rock. She said, "My Lord, save me from Pharaoh," and her soul was raised to Paradise, and the rock fell upon a body with no soul in it. Al-Ḥasan said: He raised her to Paradise where she eats and drinks. It is also said: when she said, "My Lord, build for me a house with You in Paradise," she saw her house in Paradise being built for her, and it is of a single pearl. Allah knows best how it is and what it is.

There are discussions regarding the verse:

The first discussion: What is the benefit of His saying, "from Our servants" (min ʿibādinā)? We say it has two aspects:

The first: to honor them, as has passed.

The second: to show that the servant is not preferred over the other in His sight except by righteousness.

The second discussion: What was their betrayal? We say: it was their hypocrisy, their concealment of disbelief, and their backing of the two Messengers' opponents. The wife of Noah said to her people, "He is a madman," and the wife of Lot used to inform on the arrival of Abraham's guest. It is not permissible that their betrayal was in fornication. From Ibn ʿAbbās: "The wife of a prophet never committed adultery at all." It is also said their betrayal was in religion.

The third discussion: What is the meaning of combining "ʿindaka" (with You) and "fī al-Janna" (in Paradise)? We say: she sought nearness to Allah's mercy, then specified the place of nearness by her saying "in Paradise"; or she intended the elevation of her rank in the Paradise of the Abode, which is closest to the Throne.

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Mary, daughter of ʿImrān, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our Spirit, and she affirmed the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was among the obedient.﴾ "Guarded" (aḥṣanat) means she kept herself from illicit acts, because she had been accused of fornication. The "chastity" (farj) is taken in its literal sense. Ibn ʿAbbās said: Gabriel blew into the opening of the shirt (jayb al-dirʿ), stretching it with two of his fingers and blowing into it. Everything in a garment that is torn or the like is called "farj" (opening). It was also said: "aḥṣanat" means she exerted herself in her chastity, and the muḥṣana is the chaste woman. ﴿So We breathed into her of Our Spirit﴾ means into the opening of her garment. It was also said: We created in it what makes life appear in bodies. His saying "into her" (fīhi) refers to ʿĪsā, and whoever reads "fīhā" (into her) refers to the person of ʿĪsā itself, and nafth is feminine. As for the comparison to blowing, it is because the Spirit, when it was created in him, spread through the whole body like wind when it is blown into something. It was also said: it is called blowing because of the speed of its entry into him, like the wind.

﴿And she affirmed the words of her Lord﴾. Muqātil said: this means ʿĪsā. This is supported by the reading of al-Ḥasan, "bi-kalimati rabbihā" (the word of her Lord). ʿĪsā is called "the word of God" in several places in the Qur'an. That word is expressed here in the plural. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: "the words" (al-kalimāt) are the sacred laws (sharā'iʿ) which He prescribed for her, not speech. So the meaning is: she affirmed the laws and acted upon them, and she affirmed the scriptures and did not deny them. The laws were called "words" as in His saying: ﴿And when Abraham was tested by his Lord with words﴾ (al-Baqarah: 124). As for His saying "ṣaddaqat", it is read with light and with heavy emphasis (takhfīf and tashdīd), on the basis that she made the words and scriptures truthful, meaning she described them as truthful, and this is the very meaning of "taṣdīq." "Kalimat" and "kalimati," and "kutubihi" and "kitābihi," are also read. The intended "kitāb" here is also in the sense of multiplicity and generality. His saying: ﴿And she was among the obedient (al-qānitīn)﴾: Ibn ʿAbbās said it means the obedient, and ʿAṭā' said: among those who pray. In the verse there are the following discussions:

First discussion: What are God's words and His scriptures? We say: by God's words is meant the scrolls revealed to Idrīs and others, and by His scriptures the four books. It may also mean everything God spoke to His angels and what He wrote in the Preserved Tablet and elsewhere. It is also read: "bi-kalimati Allāh wa-kitābihi," meaning with ʿĪsā and his scripture, which is the Gospel. If it is asked why "al-qānitīn" is in the masculine form, we say: because qunūt (obedience) is a quality that includes whoever is obedient of either group, so the masculine has precedence over the feminine. And "min" (among) is partitive, as stated in al-Kashshāf. It was also said: "among the obedient" because the intended group is a people, and it is general, like ﴿And bow with those who bow﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 43), meaning: be among those who persist in obedience to God Almighty. Also, she was of the descendants of Hārūn, brother of Mūsā, peace be upon them both.

As for citing the example of the wife of Nūḥ, named Wāʿilah, and the wife of Lūṭ, named Wāhilah, it contains several benefits, which none knows in full except God Almighty. Among them: a warning to men and women about the great reward and the painful punishment. Among them: knowledge that the righteousness of another does not benefit the corrupt, and the corruption of another does not harm the righteous. Among them: that a man, even if he is in the utmost righteousness, cannot feel secure regarding his wife, nor regarding himself, as with the wives of Nūḥ and Lūṭ. Among them: knowledge that a woman's chastity and purity is extremely beneficial, as it benefited Mary daughter of ʿImrān, as God related when He said: ﴿Indeed God has chosen you and purified you and chosen you﴾ (Āl ʿImrān: 42). Among them: a warning that sincere supplication in the presence of God Almighty is a means to deliverance from punishment and to reward without reckoning, and that returning to the eternal presence is necessary in every matter, and to Him is the return and the final destination. Exalted is His power and high is His word; there is no god but Him, and to Him is the final return. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds, and His blessings upon the master of the messengers, and upon his family and companions, and peace.
